analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from erasing lawsuits against people or companies that never filed for bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate's final weeks, sent to the Judiciary Committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company files for bankruptcy, courts have sometimes wiped out not just the company's debts but also lawsuits against other parties — a parent company, a corporate family, or wealthy owners who never filed for bankruptcy themselves. This bill would ban those "nonconsensual releases": a bankruptcy court could no longer discharge someone else's liability unless that person or company agreed in a signed writing, and silence or simply not objecting would not count as agreement. It would also cap temporary freezes on such lawsuits at 90 days, allow fast appeals of those freezes, and require courts to dismiss bankruptcy cases where a company deliberately split its assets from its liabilities and dumped the liabilities into the bankruptcy.
analysis.who_benefits: People who hold lawsuits against someone who didn't file for bankruptcy — for example, victims of a drug or product who are suing the owners or parent company, not just the bankrupt subsidiary. Today a bankruptcy court can erase those claims as part of a reorganization deal, often without the victims' individual agreement. This bill would keep their right to sue intact unless they personally, knowingly give it up in writing, and it would stop courts from freezing those lawsuits indefinitely while a bankruptcy plays out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tort victims suing wealthy owners or parents

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a bankruptcy court from discharging, releasing, or modifying the liability of anyone other than the debtor on claims held by others, and from issuing injunctions blocking such lawsuits.

Consent to give up a claim is valid only if given in a signed writing after clear notice; agreeing to a plan, objecting, staying silent, or doing nothing does not count as consent, and claimants cannot be treated worse for refusing.

Caps temporary stays of lawsuits against non-debtors at 90 days unless the claimant expressly agrees, and creates immediate appeal rights so stays dissolve quickly if a court of appeals does not uphold them.

Requires dismissal of a chapter 11 case where the debtor or its predecessor, within the prior 10 years, used a divisional merger or similar restructuring to separate material assets from material liabilities and park those liabilities in the bankruptcy.
Takes effect immediately and applies to cases already pending, though final orders entered before enactment are untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy families and corporate parents who currently benefit when a subsidiary's bankruptcy wipes out lawsuits against them — they would face those lawsuits again, or would have to pay more in settlement to obtain genuine written consent. Corporate debtors whose reorganization deals depend on third parties getting released would find those deals harder or impossible to confirm, and companies that used split-asset restructurings within the past decade could see their bankruptcy cases thrown out.

drawbacks.text: Nondebtor releases have sometimes been the price for a huge settlement: a third party agrees to put billions into the victims' fund only if it is permanently released from suit. An outright ban means courts cannot bless those packages even when the released party's contribution would leave victims with more money than suing them ever would.

The bill applies immediately to already-pending cases, including the 10-year lookback that forces dismissal of cases built on asset-liability splits — which could unravel reorganizations and settlements that are already in progress and leave claimants in those cases with years of added delay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core prohibition targets a practice that has repeatedly stripped ordinary claimants of their day in court against parties who never filed for bankruptcy, and the written-consent safeguards are carefully drafted so voluntary deals still work. The real costs sit in two places: settlements where a released third party's cash contribution exceeds anything victims could recover by suing them, and the retroactive application to pending cases, which injects uncertainty into reorganizations already underway. On balance the protections for claimants are strong and the objection cases are real but narrower; the retroactivity is the most contestable design choice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or markup, and the Congress ended three weeks after introduction.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 3, 2024, in the final month of the 118th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
Four senators cosponsored the bill — three Democrats and one Independent — and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill received no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no companion action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals and parent companies who can still rely on bankruptcy courts to release them from lawsuits — including in pending mega-cases — are better off because the bill died, while claimants keep no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy non-debtors shielded by bankruptcy releases

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 3, 2024, in the Senate's final month, and built a small cosponsor group.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its support was confined to four senators, all Democrats or Independent, with no Republican cosponsor.

industries.industry: Wealthy individual owners of bankrupt companies (e.g., the Sackler family, per the Purdue Pharma bankruptcy)
industries.note: The bill eliminates the tool by which a family member or owner who never filed for bankruptcy gets permanently released from victims' lawsuits as part of a subsidiary's bankruptcy deal. The practice drew national attention in the Purdue Pharma case, where opioid victims' claims against the Sacklers were the subject of a contested release in exchange for a multibillion-dollar settlement.

industries.industry: Corporate parents and mass tort defendants using 'Texas two-step' divisional restructurings
industries.note: These companies split healthy assets away from liabilities, file the liability-laden shell into chapter 11, and seek releases of claims against the parent. Section 4 lets courts dismiss such cases outright within a 10-year lookback, and Section 2 blocks the releases these structures are built to obtain.

industries.industry: Restructuring and bankruptcy legal and advisory industry
industries.note: Large-scale restructurings that currently sell courts on global releases and open-ended stays would need fundamentally different deal structures, shrinking a lucrative deal model built around resolving mass torts through bankruptcy.
